name: Free love
summary: Free love holds that sexual and romantic relationships between adults belong to the people in them, not to the state or the church: love must not be regulated by law, marriage as a legal bond is rejected as exploitative (a form of ownership of women), and women as well as men have a right to sexual desire and to control their own bodies. Its writers also fought the obscenity laws that stopped them discussing sex, contraception and marriage. In the sources it was mostly a nineteenth-century American movement of sex radicals, spiritualists, utopians and individualist anarchists, carried on by individualist anarchists and Greenwich Village bohemians; its critics charged it with promiscuity, which its defenders denied.
scope: The free-love movement as the defining sources describe it: the nineteenth-century (chiefly American, 1850s to c.1900) doctrine, held by the 'sex radicals', that sexual and romantic unions should be free of legal and religious regulation, with its critique of legal marriage, its women's-rights and anti-obscenity-law strands, and its later bohemian and anarchist carriers (Greenwich Village bohemians, Emma Goldman). Defining sources: Encyclopedia.com's 'Free Love' entry (s2: 'The prime tenet of free love held that love was sacred, and as such it must not be regulated by law'), the PBS/Mari Jo Buhle encyclopedia entry (s3: 'free love meant an absence of legal ties rather than promiscuity'), Britannica on Woodhull (s1) and Libertarianism.org on Harman (s4), plus the movement's own tract, Austin Kent's 1857 'Free love' (s6), and Ellis's hostile 1870 account (s5), used only to identify the movement and its figures. It excludes the popular sense of free love as mere promiscuity, which the sources say misdescribes the movement, and the 1960s counterculture's practice except where the sources tie it to the doctrine. It covers Noyes's Oneida 'complex marriage' only as the sources name it as part of the movement (s2, s5); no source treats it as the movement's centre.
